That is the fruits of the garden, namely the works which proceed after the planting and the watering of baptism, are to me pomegranates, that is ripe refreshment, so delighting me as paradise. Cypress. That is, straight, and growing upwards, slender and attenuated in humility, by whose works joined with charity the Prince is anointed. Cypress expresses divine grace, nard the Lord's passion, saffron charity. Cypress in Egypt is an aromatic tree with white and fragrant seed, which is cooked in oil and pressed, whence the royal ointment called cypress is prepared. So in the darkness of this world the blessing of divine grace is received in the fatness of charity and proved by the flames of temptations, with which is joined nard, a humble herb, that is faith in the Lord's passion and its imitation. Cypress is joined with nard, when divine grace strengthens us to suffer with Christ. Likewise nard is joined with saffron: when in the charity of Christ we gladly accept death. Nard is fragrant and warm, and signifies charity. Saffron is of golden color and signifies those imbued with divine wisdom.
4.14: 4.14 Calamus and cinnamon. Calamus which is also cassia, an aromatic tree, but small: it is of strong and purple bark, which avails to cure the troubles of the bowels, which for its smallness is by some reckoned among sweet-smelling herbs, which signifies the humble in spirit, who mindful of the Lord's passion are prepared to suffer for the Lord. Cinnamon is a short tree, but fragrant and sweet, of ash color, twice as good as calamus for use in medicine. And it signifies those who reckon themselves weak, whose humility has sweetness and praise with God. And well after the purple calamus is cinnamon of ash color put; because by remembrance of the Lord's passion contempt of our own virtue arises in us. Calamus and cinnamon come forth in the garden with the trees of Libanus: because in the Church those who are humble and patient with those who fortify the Church by preaching or by doing virtues await the palm of reward. With all trees. As calamus and cinnamon the humble thoughts of the saints: so also the trees of Libanus, which are high and robust, show the sublime actions and prayers of the saints. Myrrh renders the body incorruptible, and signifies those who by bitterness and patience make their body secure from carnal motions and from every adverse part. Aloes has not as much strength as myrrh, yet avails against putrefaction. With the first. That is, with the more excellent gifts of virtues. And beautiful the conjunction of herbs and trees with ointments: because while we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the spirit. In the enclosed garden of the Lord, among others it grows.
4.15: 4.15 The fountain of gardens. Which from the primitive Church went forth into the world, the heavenly doctrine, which would bring forth many churches, namely gardens. Of which fountain it is well added: A well of living waters, because the same doctrine of the Church is also the fountain of gardens, because she produces spiritual fruits in those she instructs: and a well because of the hidden mysteries which are opened to the saints alone by revelation of the Holy Spirit. Of living waters, on account of the divine utterances, which proceed from the invisible treasures of divine grace, and lead to eternal life. From Libanus, that is, from the Church herself, which is white by the cleanness of faith, and high by the grace of virtues.
4.16: 4.16 Arise. And since such is the garden, arise, that is, depart or fight. Arise. The garden planted and watered, it remained that all things being firmly and orderly composed, access of tempting be in no way denied to her adversaries, but rather it be shown that the more she is scourged, the more the inward sweetness of her waves is opened. In the north, the adversities of the world; in the south, understand the blandishments, because the Church is proved by double assault. Arise, is of one permitting, not commanding. Blow through. One by vexing, the other by refreshing. Blow through, that is, bring tribulation, or by persecuting, that the Church, struck and proved in both, may spread everywhere the wonderful odor of her constancy and more abundant virtue, and satisfy those placed at the end of the world with the unspeakable fragrance of her sweetness.
5.1: 5.1 Let my beloved come. He who promised to be with me to the consummation of the world, now when I need greater grace more, let him visit me. Let my beloved come. The Church, hearing that she is to be proved by temptations, does not contradict the providence of her beloved: but, lest she be overcome, seeks the help of him who does not suffer us to be tempted above that which we are able. 1 Corinthians 10. Or, it can be so understood from the voice of the perfect. Let my beloved come. As: As we always love him, and care to serve him: so let him not suffer us in temptations to be shaken to the point of failure, but now he will render us the reward of pious devotion. I am come into my garden. The Bridegroom, answering the desire of the Church, testifies that he has already done the very things asked: whence strangers can be greatly kindled to love of him. I am come, correcting the erring, raising the weak, confirming those who do good, placing the ripe with me in rest. I have gathered. By a certain sickle of death I cut off from this life, and led into the cellars of beatitude. I have eaten the honeycomb. By the honeycomb, those who in the Scriptures seek the sweetness of spiritual understanding, and make it clear to others; by honey, those who gladly taste the feasts of the divine word set before them, and desire to feed on these insatiably; by wine, the strong preachers of heavenly things; by milk, the weak hearers yet, who though they differ by diverse manners of study, yet the supreme judge approves as common in the one hope of the heavenly reward. Eat, O friends. Not only does he himself delight in the pious acts of the elect: but also exhorts the faithful to rejoice together over such a banquet, that they show more among themselves the mutual care of love, and the lesser strive to imitate by memory what they see in the greater. And be inebriated, my dearly beloved. GREGORY. After the drink of joy, by retreading the very virtues of the good, shake off torpor of mind, and kindled to the love of eternal things, feel not temporal pains; as the drunken, who forgets all temporal things; he eats, and is not filled: who has learned the feasts of the Scriptures, knows the examples of the just, and yet has not corrected his life; he drinks, and is not inebriated, who joyfully hears the precepts of life, but remains slow to fulfill them.
5.2: 5.2 I sleep. The Church of the Gentiles, commended in many ways, lest secure she abandon preaching, and attend to contemplation alone, is enjoined about the strengthening of others. And here he treats of that succession of the Church which is in this present world, from that time, namely, when the fullness of the Gentiles had entered until the end of the world, when the Jews will enter; and here she seems not to be sent to all manner of unbelievers, but rather to exhort those who are tepid in the Church, and so the Church herself says: I sleep. Open to me, my sister, etc. Arise from the leisure and quiet of contemplation, and open hearts, that, the obstacles of vices removed, they may admit the light of truth clearly. Of my blood, my sister; of my approach, my nearest; of my spirit, my dove; of my speech, which you have learned more fully from leisure, my perfect. My head. That is my faith, and love of me in the hearts of those blinded by love of earthly things has grown cold, and as it were wholly failed. My locks. That is the love of neighbors, who are my hairs cleaving to the head: are full of the drops of the nights, that is, they suffer the grave cold of persecution of the dark, that is of those who are both unfaithful toward me, and persecute neighbors; and for the sake of correcting these you must interrupt, interpose, the sweetness of contemplation.
5.3: 5.3 I have put off my garment. The Church not disobedient about the enjoined office, but fearing in undertaking the care of the brethren lest she fall into sins, without which this life is not passed, answers: I have put off my garment. How can it be that going out from the summit of contemplation, I be again polluted with the filth of the world, because, the care of temporal helps received, any excellent teacher hardly avoids sin. GREGORY. He who girds himself for the care of ruling souls, it remains that those to whom he preaches eternal things he must also watch to provide helps for temporal necessities.
5.4: 5.4 My beloved. The Church fearing a fall, because the Lord wishes our love toward him to be known in the greatest love of neighbors, it is aptly added: My beloved, as: I indeed fear the conversation of the world; but I understand that charity covers a multitude of sins; and I trust in the help of my beloved, by whom their hearts are already pricked. His hand. Working compunction, or, he has brought back to our memory the work which he wrought in us, because needing nothing, coming from the bosom of the Father, he willed to converse on earth for us. He puts in his hand, when by his power he strikes the mind through subtle understanding. And my belly. By the belly can be understood the softness and frailty of those who undertake the office of preaching, because they recognize themselves less fit, and fear. Belly. That is the soft and flowing part among us; or, by the name of belly the heart is designated, which as food in the belly so thoughts in the heart are digested. The heart trembles, if it refuses to do for neighbors what God did for enemies. And the belly trembles, because weakness rejoicing in heavenly understanding is troubled in its exultation, and fears lest it lose what it knows not how to hold.
5.5: 5.5 I arose to open. I arose from sleep to labor; because it is necessary that he who disposes to preach the truth first rise to do what he preaches, lest preaching to others he himself be made a reprobate; to which the words added agree, My hands dropped, etc. And my fingers were full of myrrh. Fingers, that is discretion, that by the sole regard of the heavenly reward, not for human advantage, they may be shown to work. For as in the hand are the discrete fingers: so in works discretion must be applied, otherwise they avail not.
5.6: 5.6 The bolt of the door. The cause of sin, that is unbelief, and any other: because as the bolt the door, so the cause holds sin, which removed it is removed, and sin taken away the way lies open to Christ. She had said that the Beloved, his hand put in through the opening, had touched her and shaken her with trembling: by his touch vehemently inflamed, she now desires to be touched by his hand not through the narrowness of the opening, but, the door of the heart opened, to enjoy his most happy embrace, that is to be filled more fully with the sweetness of divine illumination, which she had felt in haste, but because to none of the elect in this life is perfect vision of eternal things granted, which is reserved to the other life, it is rightly added: But he had turned aside. My soul, etc. Behold now the third degree: the primitive was converted from the Jews; through which, and after which this Gentile, of which hitherto we have treated; which Gentile, as we said, established this third, of which now he follows up: which will last until the last entering of the remnants of Israel by the succession of prelates and subjects. Pass by indeed, but yet he spoke to me leaving his commands, that I should patiently wait for him: and after he spoke, My soul melted. I sought and found him not: I called, etc. The voice of the same Church, who opened, according to those whom she opened: who before was the belly or voice of them.
5.7: 5.7 They took away my veil. GREGORY. The preachers take away the veil when, if any residue of worldly pomp was left, they remove it from the soul, or, if any sin was in it through ignorance, they uncover it.
5.8: 5.8 I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find, etc. The young maidens, now advanced to some knowledge, come devoutly to the servants of God, whom they believe to lead an angelic life on earth, and entreat them that in the time of their prayer they commend them to the Lord. You daughters of Jerusalem of the heavenly spirits, who already reign with God. Or, by the daughters of Jerusalem we can take also the inferior in the Church, whom the superiors also admonish to seek with them: because what is sought by many is sometimes found sooner, and that everywhere the charity of love be shown.
5.9: 5.9 What is your beloved. This bride recalling the inmost of conscience, is afraid, and accusing her sloth through humility hastens to labor, saying: I beseech, because you have so adjured us with the fervor of divine charity which you have, make me also burn, and in the love of him confirm me by saving admonition. Fitly, proclaiming the heralds of his virtues and power with fitting praise, she is again asked in the minds of what sort his footprints are wont to be found.
5.10: 5.10 My beloved is white and ruddy. A worthy answer to the seekers on the bride's part. My beloved. First, clean and holy he came into the world, afterward bloody by passion he went out of the world. By white, the love of the Godhead; by ruddy, take the flesh that suffered, to note God and man, and in both chosen. Chosen out of thousands. Because the one Mediator accepted from every number of angels or men; whence it is said: This is my beloved Son, etc., Matthew 3. Because no other was found, neither in heaven, nor on earth who would receive the book, Apocalypse 5.
5.11: 5.11 His head is the finest gold. Another translation: His locks are firs. Fir in Greek is called. Hence here elate seems not Latin, but Greek. Or the head, that is the Godhead, because the head of Christ is God, 1 Corinthians 11. His locks, that is, his thoughts, holy and right, and yet despicable to fools. Black as a raven. Despicable to the world, like that noisy and wicked bird. Or, like a raven, that they entrust the sacraments of the Church to no one until they see them like themselves, or their mother, or, because when they are fair they understand that they were black by their own nature.
5.12: 5.12 His eyes as doves. GREGORY. Doves are wont to sit by streams of waters, that they may see in the water the shadow of birds flying overhead, and so avoid claws: so the saints in the Scriptures foresee the frauds of the demons, and from the deception they attend to, as from a shadow, know the enemy, and flee, which streams are called most full, because on whatever counsel is sought in Scripture, through it is found fully. By the rivulets can be understood the instruction of the old law; by the streams the evangelical perfection: because preachers bring forth both new and old. His eyes. That is the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which he gives, which do not permit his lovers to wallow in mire after the manner of swine, but make them bright and clear in the likeness of waters, having nothing dark. Whence also they are compared to rivulets and clean waters, not turbid pools, because they see God, and are filled with the light of divine gifts. Which gifts, because they are given by grace alone, it is added: Which are washed with milk. Because as a mother gives milk to her children by natural love alone, so God by grace alone gives the gifts of charisms to his children. Which sit beside the most full streams of waters: because the more clearly they see of God, the more they stretch to know higher things.
5.13: 5.13 His cheeks. That is, the modesty and piety of the Savior, which shone in him singularly. As beds. As the beds are arranged by men expecting sweetness of odor and grace of appearance, so the Mediator appearing in the flesh delighted those present by the modesty and sweetness of his doctrine, drew those absent: planted by the perfumers; that is, the apostles and prophets, who in concordant voice described in the sacred pages not only his sayings but also his manners, in his future hidden incarnation, from modesty he wept for Lazarus, as a lamb he was dumb, and the like. His lips lilies dropping choice myrrh. The words of his doctrine lilies which promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom, heavy to the suffering, the first myrrh, because they preach contempt of pleasures.
5.14: 5.14 His hands. That is the works of Christ: for what he taught by word he fulfilled in work, that those wondering at his doctrine he might confirm by works. Turned, because he has ready to do what he wills, as turning is more ready than the other arts: and because he holds in himself every rule of justice, whence it is said: It behooves us to fulfill all justice in me, Matthew 3. Golden, full of hyacinths. Because the virtues which he exercised in man, the grace of divinity perfected: which excite us to hope and love of heavenly things. For the hyacinth is of an airy color. His belly of ivory, that is, the frailty of humanity: ivory for the beauty of chastity, because free from all sin. Distinguished, namely, not wholly of ivory, nor wholly of sapphire. Sapphire signifies the sublimity of heavenly things. Distinguished therefore, because partly human frailty in hunger, temptation, weariness, death, partly divine loftiness in miracles, resurrection and ascension is understood. Sapphire has the appearance of a clear sky.
5.15: 5.15 His legs are pillars, that is, the journeys of the passion, incarnation, which are called pillars on account of rectitude and firmness, because whatever was done by him was disposed by God before times. Founded upon bases. That is upon the prophets, because he appeared such as foretold by them in the divine disposition for those who read. Or the bases the very disposition of God, which ordained. His look as of Libanus. Why do I praise each member of the Redeemer himself, I will comprehend the whole briefly: as Libanus is remarkable for height and breadth; so the Lord surpasses all who have arisen from the earth. And as that mountain is fertile of noble trees, so he lifts up and preserves all the saints rooted in him; and as the cedar surpasses all the glory of the forests in beauty, strength, height, odor: so the beloved is beautiful in form above the sons of men, Psalm 44., because he received not by measure, and of his fullness we have all received, John.
5.16: 5.16 His throat most sweet, etc. That is, the inward savor and sweetness of the words of Christ, which few taste: but those who taste, hunger more. Otherwise: As through the throat the vital breath goes to the lips, that they may be able to speak, so on the lips of the Lord the words which he spoke. In the throat, however, can be understood the hidden disposition of his goodness, by which it was done that he should speak outwardly to us. All, that is God and man; desirable, not only according to divinity, but also according to humanity from the very beginning of conception, to the triumph of the passion, resurrection, ascension. Such is my beloved. As: And it is necessary if you love him, and wish to be loved by him, that you understand him such, and cleave to him with such affection. Daughters of Jerusalem. For the beauty of the song the persons conversing vary: but the same Church of Christ is marked both by the name of bride and the name of daughters. When she sighs for the heavenly country, daughter: when she cares to hear or speak nothing but God, she is called bride.
5.17: 5.17 Whither is your beloved gone. The quality of the Beloved heard, concerning which the daughters of Jerusalem had asked, they add another question: because after so many praises enumerated, who hearing would not desire? and this it behooves to inquire in the unity of holy Church, in the heart of what sort chiefly, and in what kind of conversation the Lord is wont to be found. Whither is he gone, not leaving those in whom he was, but where he may associate others, and after others invite others also, and so he is said to go away, and to turn aside, after the manner of a candle, which when kindled lights many others round about, yet itself suffers no detriment. Whither is he gone. GREGORY. It is to be known that God, who is everywhere, is in place, but is not local. That is called local which is circumscribed according to the parts of place above and below, before and behind, right and left. But since angels and human souls cannot be circumscribed by place, far less that incomprehensible substance. A greater knowledge, which can be had of God in the present, is also according to his works alone: because what is higher, in the flesh we can subtly attend to the wonder of the works of God. Whither is your beloved gone, O fairest among women. Although God is in all things in the common way, by presence, power, substance, yet in a familiar way he is said to be in, that is, by grace, those to whom his works seem more wonderful, who though they have not full knowledge of God, yet consider more keenly the wonder of the works of God.
6.1: 6.1 My beloved. He went down watering with the fountain of baptism, coming from on high he visited those placed in the lowly. That we might ascend upward, the Lord descended to the mountain, Moses ascended to the mountain. When he had said. He went down to the garden, he adds how the same garden is constituted, with what fruit fruitful, when he says, to the bed of aromatics. The garden the Church: the garden any faithful soul. The bed is the faithful mind, which taught by the discipline of right faith, is as it were composed on equal sides here and there: and as it were turned over very frequently by a skillful digging-tool, and cleansed from superfluous weeds. She answers that he is delighted with the pious desires of the saints and fruitful works, and gathers all the perfect by virtues of chastity to eternal joys. He gathers lilies, while those arriving at the whiteness of perfect merits, he brings out from the state where they were before and leads to the heavenly kingdoms.
6.2: 6.2 I to my beloved. He adds this verse exaggerating the sting of immense charity, which burns within. As: He descended into me, in me you can have the form of him whom you seek. I to my kinsman and my kinsman to me, who feeds among the lilies.
6.3: 6.3 You are beautiful, my friend. Hitherto the voice of the Church praising and seeking her Lord: who since he is not far from his lovers, it follows what he answers to the sought: and declares that he was present to them speaking, and heard what they said; and rewards the devotion toward him with worthy praise of them. Terrible as an army set in array. Because compacted by the unity of charity, she opens no place by the evil of discord to enemies, that is heretics or unclean spirits. The camps of the Romans were terrible, because they oppressed the whole world: but they were not sweet, because they had not true peace. In the Church neither terror takes away sweetness, nor sweetness terror: who on earth leads a heavenly life, and strives to draw the barbarian minds of various nations to her rite. Who nevertheless, because she has not yet deserved to behold the face of the Beloved, which she seeks most, here hears in what follows:
6.4: 6.4 Turn away your eyes from me. As: I gave you dove's eyes, with which you may discern the paths of justice: but yet in the time of your pilgrimage seek not to know me perfectly. For man shall not see me and live, Exodus 33. Seek not on the way the reward which is reserved to you in the country. Because they themselves. Cease not from desire of knowing, but presume not on the faculty of knowing: whence it is said, His greatness has no end, Psalm 144. Have made me flee away. RABANUS. The more intensely you seek to know me, the more intensely you understand me to be incomprehensible, and it is not your fault if you know me not: but the infirmity of human condition. Your hairs as a flock of goats, etc. These verses were set above, and expounded, but let it not weary us to expound again what it wearied not the author to repeat in writing, that something new may be added. That the Church bear not heavily that she is held back from the knowledge of the Beloved, there follows a description by which she is likened to that primitive Church of Jerusalem, about which it is not doubted that she was a friend of God. All with twin lambs, and there is none barren among them. With like offspring, because they make others such as they are themselves. Or double offspring, the works of twin charity, or, the faithful converted from both peoples: or, faith and work.
6.6: 6.6 As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, etc. GREGORY. When many do wonders, prophesy things to come, leave the world perfectly, burn with heavenly desires: they are compared to the rind of a pomegranate of holy Churches. But all these are nothing in comparison with the thing of which it is written: What eye has not seen nor ear heard, etc. Isaiah 64. Whence he fittingly adds: Without your hidden parts, as if he said, great indeed are the things which are not hidden in you, but very unspeakable those which are hidden.
6.7: 6.7 There are threescore queens and fourscore concubines, etc. Queens and concubines alike approach the throne of the king, alike bear children, but not both have the diadem of the kingdom. The queens are those who for the view of the heavenly kingdom serve doctrine; the concubines, who for love of temporal things announce Christ. Therefore those sixty, because by love alone of the precepts of God they have the perfection of works, which by the multiplication of twelve by five can be understood: or because they temper the five bodily senses to the rule of apostolic doctrine. Eighty, however, when taken in evil, designates the cares and entanglements of temporal things: because the course of the age also revolves in four seasons, and the world itself is divided by four quarters, east, west, north and south, or composed of four elements.
6.8: 6.8 One is my dove, my perfect one. Although the persons are many and diverse, yet the faith is one in them, one baptism, one God, one work; not one before the law, another under the law, another under grace: but constituted in one peace, one fear. Our mother is regenerating grace, which chose the simple, and keeps and lifts up the chosen. Or the mother is the heavenly Jerusalem, because every best gift comes from above, James 1., which heavenly Jerusalem approves this alone of human conversation, that it desires to serve God in the unity of her faith and love. They saw her. Great praise of Catholic unity, which both grace the mother who begot, chooses forever; and the daughters whom she herself by the Spirit begot and nourishes, soon saw, that is learned the chastity of her life. They proclaimed. Whether those who are truly partakers of the kingdom; or even those who adhere by name only, and if their hope be in earthly things, confess her worthy of praise.
6.9: 6.9 Who is she. The Church of the Gentiles so firmly established, and everywhere diffused and brought forth in her manifoldness through her degrees and successions to the last times, in those last times the Synagogue now looking on, so well wrought, and working the holy Church herself, so diffused, so many most wise following one faith without schism: besides the miracles of the living and the dead, and many other arguments of the Christian faith; now joined, penitent, and pricked, says admiringly, Who is she, etc. Rising as the morning. Then the Church becomes morning, when she utterly loses the darkness of mortality and ignorance. In judgment therefore it is still morning, but in the kingdom it will be day, where she will have the full sight of the true sun. Fair as the moon. In the night of the present life, where the states of temporal things vary, she is compared to the moon: because now bright to the world, now despised; now full of the whiteness of virtues, now dishonored by the vices of the wicked. In the future beatitude, where the same state will be, the just shall shine as the sun. Terrible as an army set in array. They have such prelates ordered for themselves, who by probable sentences make void our faith, and strike terror into us. The more perfectly she places the order of virtues in herself, the more terrible is the Church to the powers of the air, or any faithful soul.
6.10: 6.10 I went down into the garden of nuts, etc. Judea marveling at the struggles of the Church, and inquiring; the Bridegroom himself bears witness to the Church. Or, let them be said to be the words of the Church, who assents to the Synagogue praising her, and straightway intimates what is the cause to her of military array, answering from the voice of the teachers, the leaders namely of her spiritual warfare.
6.11: 6.11 I knew not, my soul. While so the Bridegroom, or the Church herself, proclaims her evangelical labors to the wondering Synagogue: she, pricked by wholesome penitence, professes that she has wandered the longer by profane blindness. Troubled me. Because of the evangelical preaching of the Church, running swiftly through the four parts of the world, and resting on the four wheels of faith: whence it was also written by four persons; but those four horses by the same spirit draw one chariot to war.
6.12: 6.12 Return. The Synagogue confessing her slowness, the Church answers consoling and exhorting: four times she says return, because the Jews wherever now dispersed in the four parts of the world are in the end to be converted. Or, return in body, return in mind from error, that you may decline from evil. Return again in body, return in mind, that you may do good, and wish not to be troubled. It is not enough to return by will, unless the return be shown to the Church. That we may behold you, That we may know the form of chastity, and the love of Christ joining us to each other, both build one house of faith in the cornerstone itself.
7.1: 7.1 What will you see in the Shulamite. While the Church admonishes the Synagogue, the Redeemer himself, assenting to her exhortations, promises he will give effect. For Elijah and Enoch would not labor in converting them, unless by the divine Scriptures and apostolic testimonies they had the certainty of their conversion. What will you see. As if he said: You grieve over the unbelief of the Synagogue; but know that in the near future she is to be converted, so that in her unfaithfulness may now no longer appear, but works of spiritual combats and virtues. How beautiful are your steps. In the preceding descriptions there is a descent from the higher to the lower, and only the higher members are commended. In this the lower are also commended, and from the lower there is an ascent to the higher; to show that that Church at the last, called together from those formerly reprobate, will yet have members not unequal to the higher; in which mention is made of steps, because she is not to be in leisure, but to advance to the contest, shown to be about to have her first beauty from the contest. How beautiful. First he praises in her the constancy of works and the mortification of pleasures: How beautiful. Saying this to the praise of the joined Church herself he turns out of sweetness, that the Jews may be the more easily converted, and the Church may labor the more for those to be converted. The joints of your thighs. Rightly after the shod steps, the joint of the thighs is praised: because through the ministry of the preachers the unanimous union of the believing peoples is perfected. Necklaces. Most clean, when these no more dissent from those, but agree in all things: and shine by the attestation of works. Which are made. Which conjunction is ordered by the art of an inscrutable counsel: for who knows why God blinded the Jews until that time. Which are made by the hand. That is, confirmed by the ineffable largesse of the Creator. Your navel. Those also among the soft, who beget, even if they cling lawfully to the world, yet announce well.
7.2: 7.2 The navel. That is, the infirmity of our mortality becomes a bowl, when having experienced our infirmity in ourselves, that others may recognize through us, we labor, or sometimes give alms. Turned, that is round and perfect: for he who gives drink to the thirsty, or offers the cup of the divine word to the erring, in order that from God the rewarder he may expect earthly wisdom: his bowl is not made by the lathe, because the work of mercy which he did he did not for the cause of lifting his frailty to God, but seeks an earthly reward. Your belly. Our belly is a heap of wheat, when mindful of our frailty, the fruits of good works, by which we are refreshed forever, we prepare for ourselves in the present life. Your belly. Though it be a lower degree, yet the wheaten refreshment will be to God, because in the lowest many, in the higher few, yet we do not say in the lowest, that is, in sin. A heap. At the bottom broader, at the top narrower it grows. So also in our actions, which the higher they are in merit, the fewer workmen of their own they find. In the lower there are more workmen. Many give alms from their possessions, few are they who leave possessions. In the heap of wheat can be understood the alms which we dispense to the poor, and well after the bowl the members of the bride are compared to a heap of wheat, that both drink and bread to be given to the poor may be signified, which can be taken equally of bodily and spiritual refreshment. In the open is doctrine the cup, in the mysteries the bread. Hedged with lilies. When all the good things we do, we do for the grace of seeing eternal brightness. And by this we stop on every side the access of our heart to the lurking enemy.
7.3: 7.3 Two breasts. Because the teachers of the unlearned preach not their own, but take from the utterances of both Testaments, which were put forth by one author: that the one shepherd himself may fill from two flocks of sheep one fold; who are compared to a roe, because it is a clean animal, remarkable in sight and speed, and cleaving the hoof, which pertains to the discernment of good and evil; and ruminates, which is to be done after discernment; twins for one concord.
7.4: 7.4 Your neck. That is, those through whom the voice goes out, and food is carried into the body, who are a tower, because they fortify others by the example of life, and adorn. In ivory, whiteness is noted. Your eyes. Who look into hidden things, that they may be able to speak out in the open, who cease not the streams of doctrine to hearers, as in the city of Heshbon the pools always abounding in waters, copiously supply water to the people at the entrance of that city. And well are the waters said to be in the gate of the city, because no one can enter the Church unless first sprinkled with the water of doctrine and baptism. Whence at the entrance of the temple of Solomon was the brazen sea, where the priests about to enter washed hands and feet. Pools. Containing many waters of wisdom and doctrine, to give drink to those who will be in the girdle of sorrow, Antichrist persecuting, which pools are in that full entering of both manifoldnesses, which will be the daughter of multitude. Nose. The most cautious discerners of good and evil, as by the nostrils odor or stench is discerned, whom no hypocrisy deceives, and hold a most eminent place. As the tower of Libanus. On a mountain it is therefore placed for watching, that enemies who come may be seen from afar: so the life of the preacher ought always to remain firm on high, that he may foresee the incursions of the malignant, that he may detect fault before it comes. Toward Damascus. Damascus the metropolis of Syria, which brought many evils on Israel, and also took captive: by this every multitude of demons, or wicked men is signified.
7.5: 7.5 Your head. Your mind, because it rules the whole body of thoughts, is high, like a mountain by conversation of life, and such a mountain, which has knowledge of circumcision, not in the removal of the flesh, but of the superfluities of the heart. The shells of the sea cut with iron send forth tears of purple color, from which collected the dye of purple color is made. The channels, which look up to the purple of the king, are the hearts of the faithful. The wool which is dipped to become the garment of the king is humility in suffering, which is joined to the channels, when the virtue of humility with constant heart and the continual memory of the Lord's blood is animated to endurance. Ever having the purple of the true king, that is the passion, in memory, and ready to imitate, that they may be raised with Christ.
7.7: 7.7 Your stature. Because the Church in the contest of the present life tastes beforehand the joys of the future life, it is added: Is like a palm tree. This is the rectitude of good working, which despises being bent to earthly things, lifts itself wholly to heavenly, and placed in the contest tends to the prize, the contest finished, to be given the palm of victory. In the lower parts it is rough, but from above it is beautiful, and bears fruit. So the Church on earth bears rough labors, but hopes in heaven to receive reward. The palm keeps its leaves: so the Church, the state of the age varying, holds the same sacraments of faith. Breasts. That is, masters, who for the capacity of hearers temper their doctrine, and make each one drunk with the fullness of the house of God, Psalm 35., to lofty things, and make hearts glad.
7.8: 7.8 I said: I will go up. As if he said: And that she has such teachers, preaching so discreetly, is not of your merit, but my gift, because I went up into the palm tree, that is I gave the Church an increase of virtues, until she come to perfection, and I take hold of its fruits; that is, so will I strengthen and multiply virtues in them that in no way can they fall, until they arrive at maturity, and thereby your breasts shall be as clusters of cypress, because those who know little, if they announce kindly, are sometimes made drunk with a greater wisdom. I said. As: one must press on to the conversion of the Jews, because so fair a union is to follow, and because for them chiefly I suffered, because I had provided that they should be saved. Its fruits. The fruit of the Cross may be called the resurrection, and ascension, the coming of the Holy Spirit, and the salvation of the world: and by these the teachers are made drunk and strengthened. And the odor of your mouth. The odor is compared to apples, the throat to wine: because apples gain praise from newness, wine from age. As wine excels apples, so the present address of the Church excels the very fame which the speech of hearers can spread of her. The odor in the throat, the voice of present doctrine. In the odor the fame of the absent is designated: and therefore the former is compared to wine for the fragrance of virtues, the latter to apples for the sweetness of absent fame.
7.9: 7.9 Worthy of my beloved. The word which my beloved put in my mouth is of such sublimity that it ought to have been preached to the world by no other than the Bridegroom himself: because no other was found who would loose the book, and from him others received, Christ as it were drank, because, the divinity teaching, he quickly advanced in the perfection of knowledge, and gladly endured the passion, the members not in the same manner. While the Bridegroom praises the throat of the bride, she understanding that in the throat is designated the word by which salvation is given to the world: wishing from great love to dispense the word, seizes the words from the mouth of the Bridegroom, he compared her to the best wine, she added, Worthy of my beloved. To ruminate. Not so easy for drinking, that he first praying offered to others, but to be meditated with labor and zeal.
7.10: 7.10 I to my beloved. The whole zeal of my service and devotion I refer to him, and in the present life, lest I fail by laboring, he helps me: and at the end he will receive me with him to joys. I, first an exile from God, from all error am converted to God, as citizen and domestic, and he himself, first angry with the human race, is turned to me, having put on the nature of my mortality.
7.11: 7.11 Come, my beloved. You who placed in heaven the humanity assumed for me, visit me by the presence of divine grace: that I may be able to scatter the seed of your word in the field of the world, and establish the villages of cohabitation in one faith. Come. The Church seeing that neither to work well or go forth is she sufficient of herself, nor to persevere in good, or discern how much the hearers have profited, implores help. In the field, Christians; in the villages, pagans; in the vineyards, Churches; in the flowers, faith; in the fruits, virtues; in the pomegranates, martyrdom is designated. In each of these the bride seeks the presence of her beloved.
7.12: 7.12 Let us get up early. Because the night of unbelief is passed, and the light of faith appears, proceeding from the morning resurrection of Christ: from the very morning of the resurrection let us labor, in inspiring, and I in preaching. Let us see. That I, who am the tutor of little ones, may be able to discern those who have been acquired, how they bear themselves, how much they advance: that I may understand how they are to be nourished. It is not to be looked at whether the vineyards flower, but whether the flowers grow strong to bear fruit; because it is no wonder if one begins good things, but it is a great wonder if with right intention he perseveres in good work. There will I give you my breasts. That is where, to see the vineyards, and whether the pomegranates flower, we shall have come in your service: and I will show the deeds and words of my preachers in the likeness of a diligent nurse.
7.13: 7.13 The mandrakes. Rightly she calls on the Bridegroom to help the preaching, where the preachers burn with outstanding virtues. The gates, the apostles and their successors. Mandrakes, that is their virtues, which are apt as medicines: which bring quiet against the cares of the world, which exclude nausea of the word of God, which cause vices to be cut off from men without pain, which bring forth fruits, that is Churches, sweetly fragrant in confessors, like pomegranates in martyrs: they gave odor, because by the examples of the greater the lesser are confirmed. I have kept for you. Or I have kept, that is I understood all the precepts and testimonies, or the promises of both Testaments to have been given by you, or, I knew all the fruits, that is the just of both Testaments, to have been justified through you alone incarnate.
8.1: 8.1 Who will give me. Judea is brought in, now inspired and taught, and with the highest desire seeks out God. Without. Within was the Beloved, while in the beginning was the Word: without, while the Word was made flesh, John 1. That I may kiss you, etc. That is that I may see face to face, and speak mouth to mouth.
8.2: 8.2 There you will teach me. You will increase grace in me, and I, not ungrateful, will increase service.
8.3: 8.3 His left hand. That is the mystery of the incarnation, and the gifts which he gives in the present, will be under the head: because sustained by them in the present against worldly disturbances she rests, and in a way sleeps with him; and the right hand: that is the future goods, that is his full vision, will embrace me, that is, so compass me on all sides that no whirlwind of misery can intervene.
8.4: 8.4 I adjure you. The Bridegroom, hearing that last Church wish to sleep in the present, and at some time to rest; and seeing many born of the Church who disturb others; admonishes them to desist from disturbances. Till she please. Till, the duties of divine service completed, she, admonished by the needs of human frailty, consent to return to the common care.
8.5: 8.5 Who is she? Judea burning into so great love of the Bridegroom acknowledged, the Gentile, admiring and congratulating, says: Who is she? Under the tree. To the Gentiles admiring answers he who is our peace, who made both one: and admonishes to remember the grace by which she herself was snatched, and to rejoice together in the salvation of others. I raised you up. Which was the effect of great kindness, because under that tree your mother was inwardly blinded, from when she said: His blood be upon us, and upon our children, Matthew 27.
8.6: 8.6 Put me. We set Christ as a seal upon the heart, when we so learn what he said, as if they were truly words of divine wisdom. We are wont to carry about some sign tied to the finger or arm, by which we are admonished of that thing of which we wish to have more frequent memory. We set him as a sign upon the arm when we strive to hear and follow what he did as if they were truly examples of virtue. For love is strong as death. After the corruption of the mother, it is aptly added about love, that it may not be shown to be given to the Church by merits. As death. As death separates the soul from the body, so the love of God from the love of temporal things. Hard as hell, etc. Because by no temptations of enemies could he be recalled from care of our salvation: as hell is mitigated by no torments of the wretched, nor changed from the severity of its sentence. The harsher the comparison, the keener is commended the affection of the Lord who is jealous for us. Its lamps. That is the hearts of the faithful, in which love is contained as in a vessel, are fire: because inwardly they glow with love of God and neighbor. They are also flame, because outwardly they shine with works of justice. These lamps are not extinguished at the coming of the Bridegroom.
8.7: 8.7 Many waters, etc. Because the house which is founded on the rock of charity cannot fall when floods rush on. Floods. Of temptations, which either visibly or invisibly tempt the hearts of the faithful. If a man shall give. Because where love of eternal things abounds, soon possession of passing things grows cheap, rightly it is added, If a man shall give. The apostles, and other saints, all things left, seemed to themselves to have lost nothing, provided they could have the true goods, whence Paul: I count all things as dung, that I may gain Christ, Philippians 3.
8.8: 8.8 Our sister, etc. O you my ministers and fellow soldiers, this Church is new and tender to hold the new love. Our little sister. The Church, before she grows by increases of virtues, cannot offer to weak hearers the breasts of preaching; she is called grown when joined to the word of God, filled with the Holy Spirit, through the ministry of preaching she is made fruitful in the conception of sons, whom by exhorting she carries, by converting she brings forth. What shall we do to our sister, etc. As if he should plainly say: Small indeed in number is the Church of the Gentiles, and not yet sufficient to undertake the ministry of the word. What then does it seem to you, O Synagogue, is to be done toward the care of her, our sister, at that time in which I shall begin to address her through my apostles, and the successors of the apostles? Whether, as to a little one yet, we shall commit to her small secrets of heavenly mysteries, or now make her greater by increases, that, advancing well, she may be capable of more perfect virtues? To her silent, and rather listening to what he himself wishes, he at once opens what ought to be done, adding thus:
8.9: 8.9 If she be a wall, etc. If anyone shall be found who can defend others from the incursions of the erring, by strongly resisting the arms of wickedness, either fortified by natural wit or imbued with philosophical knowledge: let us form him with the divine Scriptures. If a door. If anyone is not so imbued for repelling the sophisms of heretics, but yet by simplicity of faith is able to open the right way to those wishing to enter the courts of the heavenly country, by preaching, and imbuing the little ones: let us set before him the unfading examples of former men, by which he may better fulfill his office.
8.10: 8.10 I am a wall. Now he speaks in common of the whole Church begun from the foundation of the apostles, because from then there were breasts in the Church, down to the last times. I am a wall. The Church, hearing these counsels, or promises of her Redeemer, now no longer waits one for another, but each answers for himself with devout voice. Since. All these things I could not have from myself, but since he granted me the gift of his peace, through the word of his reconciliation. As one finding peace. Well I say finding peace, because in that peace of which I spoke the vineyard was established for Christ the peaceful: which was once foretold by the law and the prophets. Which peace contains not only one people of the Jews, but has many peoples collected from the whole world, not by any merits of men, but by the peace alone which he came to make between God and man: of which vineyard, because the Lord has care, and because it is useful for men to become partakers of it, it is rightly added:
8.11: 8.11 He let it out to keepers. There follows the voice of the Peacemaker himself, which shows how great care he has of this vineyard, and what he preserves forever for those leaving their own, and what singular reward he disposes for its teachers.
8.12: 8.12 A thousand are yours, O peaceful. Whatever he has is a perfect price. By a thousand, perfection; by silver, everything worldly is understood: which indeed is sometimes small in you, but great in devotion. A thousand, etc. The same perfection which is signified by a thousand is noted also by a hundred, because each number is perfect, and the same avails for two hundred as if he said two thousand. A thousand, etc. The same is of the silver and the peaceful: because money spent for God reconciles peace between God and man.
8.13: 8.13 You that dwell in the gardens. The Church, or any faithful soul, dwells in gardens; who is now filled with the greenness of hope and good works. For dry is the hope of this world, because all things which are loved here with haste wither: She therefore who dwells in gardens must make the Bridegroom hear her voice, that is send forth the goods of preaching so far as he delights whom she desires; because the friends listen, namely all the elect, who to revive for the heavenly country desire to hear the words of life. You that dwell. And since to each is reserved with me a reward according to merits, and a double return to teachers: therefore while the time of meriting is present, while the wedding day is deferred, as much as each can, let him persist in the cultivation of this vineyard. Friends. That is the angels, whom I gave you as helpers; and the spirits of the just, who already are with God, and pray for the brethren. Make me hear. I require of you that you dwell, to depart with no tumult; afterward I also require that you make me hear your voice.
8.14: 8.14 Flee, my beloved. The Church, assenting, answers: As long as you will, be absent: defer your presence; I with long-suffering hope will bear or do whatever you command. Flee, my beloved. She speaks not desiring, for why should he whom she loves flee? but mindful of her condition, she consents to his will. Flee, my beloved. As: You indeed, who have been made comprehensible from flesh, by your divinity exceed the understanding of our sense, and in yourself remain to us incomprehensible. This the Church cries to the Lord in the prophetic spirit, after she described the death and resurrection of the Lord and his ascension. We are said to flee when what we wish to remember does not occur: when what we wish we do not hold in memory. Be like. So flee that very often by the grace of compunction you appear to the hearts of the faithful; who are the mountains of aromatics, because despising all cupidities, and vices purged, they are held by love of heavenly things, and are fragrant with the odor of virtues, and are the good odor of Christ.
